questions.prompt: A worried parent asks: 'My mother has advanced dementia and barely recognizes anyone -- does hylomorphism mean her soul, her real personhood, is somehow gone or diminished?' What is the real, careful pastoral answer?
choices: No -- the soul remains fully present as the body's form; dementia limits how it's expressed, not the soul's own presence or dignity
Yes -- once someone can no longer recognize others, hylomorphism holds their soul has effectively already departed
No -- because hylomorphism actually has no real bearing on questions like dementia at all
Yes -- a person's real dignity is only present so long as their mental capacities remain fully intact
questions.correctAnswer: No -- the soul remains fully present as the body's form; dementia limits how it's expressed, not the soul's own presence or dignity
questions.explanation: This is a real, pastorally urgent application of hylomorphism -- the soul is the whole body's own real form, present as long as the body lives, not something that fades with cognitive decline. Damage to the brain limits how the soul's powers can be expressed through it, but never diminishes the soul's own real presence or the person's own real dignity.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's earlier level on human dignity being rooted in something deeper than a person's own current abilities.

questions.prompt: Aquinas holds that no two angels can belong to the same species -- each angel is its own species. Given that individuation among bodily things comes from matter (this particular chunk of matter, marked out by quantity, makes two otherwise-identical statues two things rather than one), what does this imply about angels, who have no matter at all?
choices: Since angels lack the matter that individuates members of a species from one another, each angel cannot merely be one instance of a shared angelic nature -- it must simply BE its own distinct nature, making every angel its own species
Angels must therefore all be numerically identical to one another
Angels must be composed of a finer, invisible kind of matter to remain individually distinct
The question of angelic individuation has no bearing on their nature as pure spirits
questions.correctAnswer: Since angels lack the matter that individuates members of a species from one another, each angel cannot merely be one instance of a shared angelic nature -- it must simply BE its own distinct nature, making every angel its own species
questions.explanation: This follows directly from Act and Potency (level 2) and Causality (level 3): matter is what makes two things of the same kind numerically distinct. Remove matter entirely, as with angels, and the only way to have many distinct angels is for each one to differ in kind, not just in number -- an implication most people never draw out even after granting that angels are immaterial.
questions.hint: Ask what actually makes two members of the same species different individuals in the first place -- then ask what happens when that's taken away entirely.

questions.prompt: True or false: the Catechism teaches that angels are purely spiritual creatures, possessing intelligence and will, but denies that they are properly personal beings since personhood requires a body.
questions.explanation: The Catechism explicitly calls angels 'personal and immortal creatures' -- personhood, on this account, tracks having intellect and will, not having a body. This is a live philosophical distinction: human persons are body-soul composites, but bodiliness is not what makes something a person in the first place.
questions.hint: The Catechism uses the word 'personal' about angels directly -- check what it actually says.

citations.quote: As purely spiritual creatures, angels have intelligence and will: they are personal and immortal creatures, surpassing in perfection all visible creatures, as the splendor of their glory bears witness.

questions.prompt: Human souls are 'subsistent forms' that are nonetheless the form OF a body (hylomorphism -- soul and body as one substance). How does an angel's status as a subsistent form differ from this?
choices: An angel's form does not inform any matter at all -- it does not complete a body to make one substance the way a human soul does; it simply IS a complete substance on its own, with no material principle whatsoever
There is no real difference -- angels are simply human souls that never received a body
Angels have bodies made of a rarer kind of matter than humans do
An angel's form is less real or less actual than a human soul's form
questions.correctAnswer: An angel's form does not inform any matter at all -- it does not complete a body to make one substance the way a human soul does; it simply IS a complete substance on its own, with no material principle whatsoever
questions.explanation: A human soul is a subsistent form that is still ordered to informing a body -- it is the form of something. An angel's form is not the form OF anything material; it is a complete substance in itself. This is why the death and eventual resurrection of the body matters for humans in a way that has no angelic parallel at all.
questions.hint: The human soul, even though subsistent, is still ordered toward a body in a way an angel's nature never is.

questions.prompt: How does angelic knowledge differ from human knowledge, on the classical account this topic has been building toward since 'Being and Reason' (level 1)?
choices: Angels know by direct intellectual intuition, grasping truths immediately and wholly, rather than by the step-by-step discursive reasoning -- gathering evidence, moving premise to conclusion -- that embodied human knowers require
Angels do not possess genuine knowledge at all, only instinct
Angels know only what has been directly revealed to them by God, with no natural capacity to reason
There is no meaningful difference between angelic and human knowledge
questions.correctAnswer: Angels know by direct intellectual intuition, grasping truths immediately and wholly, rather than by the step-by-step discursive reasoning -- gathering evidence, moving premise to conclusion -- that embodied human knowers require
questions.explanation: Human reasoning is discursive because we are embodied knowers who must move from sense experience, step by step, toward abstract truth. An angel's intellect, not tied to a body's sensory apparatus, is traditionally held to grasp intelligible truth immediately -- one more consequence of the same immateriality this whole level has been tracing out.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of knowing needs a body's senses to gather evidence first, and which doesn't.

questions.prompt: The Catechism teaches that Satan and the other demons were created good by God but became evil by their own doing -- a free, ______ choice made at the moment of testing, not a nature God made evil from the start.
questions.explanation: This is a load-bearing distinction against any dualism that would make an evil spiritual principle co-equal with God: the Church teaches a radical evil spirit is a fallen good creature, not an eternal rival power. The Catechism specifically calls the angels' choice irrevocable -- unlike embodied humans, who reason discursively over time and can repent, an angel's intellect grasps its choice totally and at once, which is part of why classical theology holds that choice, once made, cannot be undone.
questions.hint: The word describes a choice that, once made by a purely intellectual nature, cannot be taken back.

questions.prompt: A skeptic asks: 'if angels have no bodies, how can Scripture describe them appearing, moving, and even wrestling (as with Jacob), as if they were located somewhere?' What is the standard Catholic philosophical answer?
choices: An angel is present at a place through the exercise of its power and operation there, not through occupying space the way a body does -- 'location' for a pure spirit means acting at a place, not filling it with extended matter
Angels temporarily grow physical bodies made of ordinary matter whenever they need to appear
These accounts describe hallucinations rather than any real angelic presence
Angels are actually made of a very thin, gas-like matter, which is why they can be located
questions.correctAnswer: An angel is present at a place through the exercise of its power and operation there, not through occupying space the way a body does -- 'location' for a pure spirit means acting at a place, not filling it with extended matter
questions.explanation: This is a classic application of act and potency to a hard case: a body is 'in' a place by filling it with extended matter, but a pure spirit, having no extension, can only be 'in' a place by acting there. Scripture's angelic appearances describe a real, active presence without requiring angels to have bodies after all.
questions.hint: Ask what 'being somewhere' could possibly mean for something that has no size or shape to begin with.

questions.prompt: Colossians 1:16 lists 'thrones, dominions, principalities, powers' as created through and for Christ. Philosophically, what does the existence of a real hierarchy of angelic natures (not just angels as a single undifferentiated group) fit with, from earlier in this topic?
choices: The Transcendentals (level 4): if each angel is its own species, a real hierarchy of distinct kinds -- greater and lesser degrees of perfection, closeness to God, and scope of operation -- follows naturally rather than needing a separate explanation
It contradicts the claim that angels are immaterial
It implies angels are actually organized into a democracy with elected leaders
It has no connection to anything else in the topic
questions.correctAnswer: The Transcendentals (level 4): if each angel is its own species, a real hierarchy of distinct kinds -- greater and lesser degrees of perfection, closeness to God, and scope of operation -- follows naturally rather than needing a separate explanation
questions.explanation: Once every angel is granted to be its own species (this level's opening claim), a graded hierarchy of angelic natures -- traditionally systematized as the nine choirs -- stops being an arbitrary add-on and becomes almost expected: distinct species differ in degree of perfection by definition, the same transcendental logic already covered when this topic discussed being, goodness, and perfection as convertible.
questions.hint: This connects back to the level about being, goodness, and degrees of perfection as really the same thing looked at differently.

questions.prompt: Why does classical theology hold that a fallen angel's rebellion, unlike a human sinner's, cannot be repented of and undone?
choices: Because an angel's intellect grasps a choice totally and immediately rather than discursively over time, its act of will is correspondingly total and fixed at once -- there is no gradual process of reconsideration the way an embodied, time-bound human deliberates and can still change course
Because God specifically decided to forgive humans but not angels, for no philosophical reason
Because angels are incapable of choice altogether
Because demons are more numerous than angels who remained faithful
questions.correctAnswer: Because an angel's intellect grasps a choice totally and immediately rather than discursively over time, its act of will is correspondingly total and fixed at once -- there is no gradual process of reconsideration the way an embodied, time-bound human deliberates and can still change course
questions.explanation: This ties directly back to the earlier question on angelic cognition: because an angel doesn't reason step by step the way humans do, its choice isn't provisional or revisable in the way a human decision, made over time and under changing information, can be. The finality is a consequence of the very same immateriality that makes angels angels in the first place, not an arbitrary extra harshness.
questions.hint: This connects to how angels know things -- all at once, not gradually -- and what that implies about how they choose.

questions.prompt: The Catechism assigns angels a real role in salvation history -- guarding, announcing, and serving -- rather than treating them as a philosophical curiosity with no bearing on ordinary faith. What does CCC 336 specifically affirm?

That angels only appear during the Old Testament period and have no role in the life of the Church today
That belief in guardian angels is a pious legend with no basis in Catholic teaching
That every human being eventually becomes an angel after death
questions.correctAnswer: That from infancy to death, human life is surrounded by the watchful care and intercession of angels, each person having an angel as guardian and shepherd leading them to life
questions.explanation: This is the point of grounding all this metaphysics in the Catechism rather than treating it as philosophy for its own sake: the doctrine of guardian angels is not decorative. It is the same metaphysical picture built across this whole level -- real, personal, immaterial creatures -- applied to something the Church actually asks the faithful to trust and pray with.
questions.hint: This is the Catechism's teaching on guardian angels specifically.
